title: How We Keep Our GlusterFS Builds Honest
summary: We build from identified upstream source, keep packaging and image changes visible, preserve hashed build evidence, and test GlusterFS artifacts three times before release.
author: Eliware
content:
# How We Keep Our GlusterFS Builds Honest

Storage software deserves a higher standard of trust than a download button. GlusterFS runs close to the operating system, network, and filesystem, and it may hold the data that keeps an application alive. Users should not have to take our word for what is inside an Eliware package or container image.

They should be able to follow the source, inspect the build evidence, verify the signatures and hashes, and see the tests the final artifact passed.

That is the standard we are building toward with the Eliware GlusterFS Repository.

## The promise

We build from identified upstream GlusterFS source revisions. We do not intentionally inject malware, spyware, viruses, backdoors, or undisclosed functionality into GlusterFS packages or images.

We keep the distinction between upstream source, packaging inputs, and image-layer additions visible. We record the build and validation process, hash the relevant evidence, sign the artifacts through the configured release process, and publish provenance for the resulting generation.

That does not mean software can be made magically risk-free. No smoke test proves the absence of every vulnerability, and no repository should ask users to replace verification with trust. Our promise is more concrete:

> Make the path from source to artifact visible, make the release process repeatable, and make the final bytes identifiable.

## Source first

The build begins with an identified GlusterFS source revision. The upstream project remains the source of the filesystem; Eliware provides a packaging, validation, and distribution layer around selected builds.

We do not secretly modify the GlusterFS source or add undisclosed code to it. The source revision is recorded as a build input so the package and image can be connected back to a known point in the upstream project’s history.

There is an important distinction here. Distribution packaging may legitimately include service integration, dependency metadata, configuration, filesystem layout, or other changes needed to install software on a target operating system. A container image may include an operating-system base, runtime dependencies, and entrypoint configuration. Those inputs are not the same thing as silently changing the GlusterFS source.

Our rule is simple:

- upstream source is identified;
- packaging changes are treated as packaging inputs;
- image-layer additions are treated as image inputs; and
- undisclosed code injection is not part of the release process.

If a patch or packaging change is intentional, it should be attributable to the build inputs rather than hidden inside a generated artifact.

## Evidence should survive the build

A package filename and version string are not enough to reconstruct what happened. Our release records capture the relationships among the source, build environment, generated packages, tests, signatures, and final image.

Depending on the artifact, that evidence includes:

- the upstream source revision;
- distribution and architecture targets;
- base-image references;
- package and image inputs;
- build commands and environment details;
- standard output and error logs;
- generated package lists;
- checksums and artifact identities;
- test results and lifecycle reports;
- signing results; and
- the final immutable image digest.

Build logs and metadata are hashed so that a later reader can detect whether the recorded evidence changed after the build. The hash is not a substitute for publishing the evidence. It is an integrity reference for the evidence that accompanies the release.

The purpose is practical. During an incident, review, or reproducibility exercise, an operator should be able to ask:

- Which source revision produced this artifact?
- Which build inputs were used?
- What happened during the build?
- Which tests passed?
- Which exact package or image was signed?
- Does the image I pulled match the image that was tested?

## Three tests, at three different points

We do not stop testing when compilation succeeds. The release pipeline uses three smoke-test stages because each stage catches a different class of failure.

```text
package build
      ↓
Smoke 1: packages before signing
      ↓
Smoke 2: signed artifacts in clean containers
      ↓
Smoke 3: final immutable runtime image
```

A passing test at one stage does not make the next stage redundant.

## Smoke 1: test the packages before signing

The first test runs against the freshly built packages before they receive the additional trust signal of signing and publication.

The packages are installed and exercised in the build or validation environment. The test checks the basic path:

- the packages install together;
- dependencies resolve;
- expected GlusterFS commands are available;
- required services start;
- peers can form a test relationship;
- a test volume can be created and started;
- the volume can be mounted or accessed;
- test data can be written and read; and
- the test resources can be removed.

The purpose is to catch immediate packaging failures before the artifact is signed. A package that cannot install or complete a basic GlusterFS lifecycle should not proceed as if it were a valid release candidate.

This test is close to the build, which makes failures easier to diagnose. It is not the final user simulation, which is why the next stages exist.

## Smoke 2: test signed artifacts in clean containers

The second test installs the signed package artifacts into clean containers representing the supported target distribution flavors. The clean environment matters because a builder can contain caches, tools, source trees, and state that hide installation mistakes.

This stage checks that the artifacts a user receives can work outside the build workspace:

- repository metadata and signatures are usable;
- the signed packages install into a clean filesystem;
- dependencies are available in the target environment;
- GlusterFS services start without builder-only state;
- a peer and test volume can be created;
- the volume can be used by a client; and
- the test environment can be cleaned up afterward.

Testing more than one supported container flavor helps catch assumptions that are invisible on a single distribution. Package names, service integration, dependencies, filesystem locations, and security defaults can differ even when the underlying GlusterFS version is the same.

The exact target matrix belongs with the release metadata. The goal is not to claim that one successful container test covers every Linux distribution. The goal is to test the actual distribution targets we publish and identify them clearly.

## Smoke 3: test the final immutable image

The third test runs against the final runtime image—the image a user is expected to pull—not merely the packages that were used to assemble it.

The test confirms that:

- GlusterFS is already present in the image;
- expected binaries, packages, and runtime components exist;

- the image starts with its intended entrypoint and configuration;
- the service lifecycle works from the assembled image;
- a test volume can be created, mounted, used, and removed; and
- the tested image identity matches the published immutable digest.

This catches image-specific failures such as missing files, incorrect permissions, broken entrypoints, incomplete runtime dependencies, or configuration that worked in a package container but not in the final image.

The principle is worth stating plainly:

> Test the thing users actually install or pull.

A package test is not an image test. An image build is not an image validation result.

## Signing answers one question, not every question

Signing is an important part of the release process, but it has a specific meaning. A valid signature helps answer:

> Did this artifact come from the holder of the expected signing key, and was it changed after it was signed?

A signature does not prove that the source is bug-free, that every dependency is safe, or that the artifact is suitable for every workload. That is why signatures are paired with source tracking, build logs, hashes, tests, and provenance.

The same applies to an image digest. A digest identifies exact image content. It does not by itself tell you whether the image was built from the intended source or tested correctly. The source record and validation evidence complete that story.

## What “no shady modifications” means

We want to be explicit because vague security language is not useful. Eliware does not intentionally add malware, spyware, viruses, backdoors, or undisclosed functionality to GlusterFS packages or images.

We also do not want “unmodified” to be misunderstood as “the package contains nothing except a raw source checkout.” Normal distribution packaging can add build metadata, dependencies, service integration, configuration, and filesystem layout. A container image can add an operating-system base and runtime support. Those changes should be visible as build inputs and should not be confused with secretly altering the GlusterFS source.

The responsible claim is therefore:

> We build from identified source, track packaging and image-layer inputs, do not intentionally inject malicious or undisclosed functionality, and preserve evidence for the resulting artifacts.

That is a process claim that can be inspected. It is more meaningful than saying “trust us” or “nothing could ever go wrong.”

## What we cannot promise

Transparency is not the same as perfection. This process does not prove:

- that the software contains no undiscovered vulnerability;
- that every dependency is free from a vulnerability;
- that a smoke test represents every customer workload;
- that a container test reproduces every host kernel or network;
- that a rolling build is appropriate for production;
- that a signed artifact is safe for every environment; or
- that replication, snapshots, or an image replace independent backups.

Users should still verify signatures and hashes, pin stable versions or immutable image digests, review the provenance available for the release, test the artifact in their own environment, and apply their organization’s security controls.

Honesty requires describing those limits alongside the process.

## What users should be able to verify

For a published artifact, the useful verification path is:

1. Identify the release lane, target operating system, architecture, and GlusterFS version.
2. Verify repository metadata and package signatures.
3. Check the package or image checksum.
4. Record the immutable image digest when using a container.
5. Find the source revision and build inputs associated with the generation.
6. Review the available build logs and their hashes.
7. Review the three smoke-test results.
8. Install or pull the artifact in a disposable environment and run your own checks.

The exact commands depend on the package manager, image registry, and release format. The repository should provide those commands alongside the artifact rather than expecting users to reverse-engineer them.

## Why we publish the evidence

We are building infrastructure that we use ourselves. GlusterFS-backed storage supports parts of the build and publication workflow, which gives us a reason to test the paths we ask users to trust. But self-hosting alone is not evidence.

The evidence is the combination of:

- known source inputs;
- visible packaging and image inputs;
- recorded and hashed build logs;
- package tests before signing;
- clean-container tests after signing;
- final immutable-image tests;
- signed metadata; and
- identifiable artifact digests.

Each piece has limits. Together, they make the release process harder to alter silently and easier for someone else to investigate.

## Our trust promise

Our promise is not that software can be made risk-free or that a test suite can anticipate every failure. Our promise is that the path from source to artifact should be visible, the release process should be repeatable, and the evidence should survive the build.

If you install an Eliware GlusterFS package or pull one of our images, you should be able to determine:

- what it is;
- where it came from;
- what changed at the packaging and image layers;
- how it was tested;
- which exact bytes you received; and
- which limitations still require your own review.

That is how we are trying to earn trust: not by asking for blind confidence, but by making the work inspectable. Read [Why We Built a GlusterFS Repository for EL10, Rolling Releases, and Containers](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/) for the broader packaging story, then visit the [Eliware GlusterFS Repository](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/) to inspect the artifacts and release information.
